LESSON OBJECTIVE
Solve advanced absolute value equations by checking signs, splitting into valid cases, and verifying every candidate in the original equation.
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
Absolute value measures distance from zero. Therefore |A| is always nonnegative. An equation |A| = B can have solutions only where B is nonnegative.
KEY DEFINITIONS

Candidate solution: a value obtained from one algebraic case. Extraneous solution: a candidate that fails the original equation. Breakpoint: a value where an expression inside absolute value equals zero.
CORE RULE
If |A| = c with c >= 0, solve A = c and A = -c. If |A| = B(x), first require B(x) >= 0, solve A = B and A = -B, and check each candidate.
HOW IT WORKS

For one absolute value, split into two equations. For several absolute values, locate all breakpoints, solve a linear equation on each interval, and keep only answers in that interval. For nested absolute values, solve from the outside inward.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — TWO BRANCHES
Solve |2x - 5| = 7. Case 1: 2x - 5 = 7 gives x = 6. Case 2: 2x - 5 = -7 gives x = -1. Check: |12 - 5| = 7 and |-2 - 5| = 7.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — VARIABLE ON BOTH SIDES
Solve |2x - 5| = x + 1. Require x >= -1. The equations 2x - 5 = x + 1 and 2x - 5 = -(x + 1) give x = 6 and x = 4/3. Both make the right side nonnegative and satisfy the original.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — REJECT AN EXTRANEOUS ROOT
Solve |x + 3| = 2x - 1. Require x >= 1/2. Case 1 gives x = 4; case 2 gives x = -2/3, which fails the required sign. The only solution is x = 4.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — TWO DISTANCES
Solve |x - 1| + |x + 2| = 5. Break at -2 and 1. For x <= -2, the equation becomes -2x - 1 = 5 and gives -3. Between -2 and 1 the sum is 3. For x >= 1, 2x + 1 = 5 gives 2. Solutions: -3 and 2.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5 — NESTED ABSOLUTE VALUE
Solve ||x - 2| - 3| = 1. First |x - 2| - 3 = +/-1, so |x - 2| = 4 or 2. Then x = -2, 6, 0, or 4. Each makes the outer absolute value equal 1.
WORKED EXAMPLE 6 — AN INTERVAL OF SOLUTIONS
For |x - 2| + |x + 2| = 4, every x between -2 and 2 works because (2 - x) + (x + 2) = 4. Outside this interval the distance sum is larger. Answer: -2 <= x <= 2.
DESMOS STRATEGY

Enter: y = abs(x - 1) + abs(x + 2) and y = 5. Look for: intersections at (-3, 5) and (2, 5). Use it to answer: x = -3 and x = 2. Why it works: intersections represent inputs where the two sides are equal. Faster or not? Desmos is useful for checking multi-absolute-value equations; splitting cases is more reliable for exact parameter or interval answers. Algebra check: at -3, 4 + 1 = 5; at 2, 1 + 3 = 5.
COMMON MISTAKES

Do not assume |A| = B always has two answers. Do not accept a candidate when B is negative. Do not forget that distance sums can equal a constant on an entire interval. Never discard a solution interval just because it is not a single number.
EXAM STRATEGY

For a variable right side, impose its nonnegative condition before branching. For a sum of absolute values, mark breakpoints on a number line and solve interval by interval. Verify all candidates against the original equation.
QUICK CHECK
Try |x - 4| = 0: x = 4. Try |x - 4| = -2: no solution because absolute value is never negative. Try |x - 4| = 3: x = 1 or 7.
LESSON RECAP
Absolute value means distance. Branch for one absolute value, split at breakpoints for sums, work outward-in for nesting, and always check the original equation.
